Many of its claims handlers have worked there for decades and take pride in spotting false claims by talking to customers face to face. After two years of falling profit, and with a new online insurer winning customers who never visit a branch, the board appointed a new chief executive. She plans to move claims onto a phone app and close 24 of the 60 branches. At present 600 handlers deal with 90,000 claims a month; after the change, 480 handlers are expected to deal with 96,000. Of the 120 handler posts that go, 70 people will retrain as app-support staff and 50 will leave. The chief executive wants the change completed in 6 months; the human resources director has proposed 24. The firm's risk register scores each risk from 1 to 5 for likelihood and for impact: typhoon closes head office (likelihood 4, impact 2); claims system fails (likelihood 3, impact 5); chief actuary leaves (likelihood 3, impact 4). The chief actuary, who prices every policy, retires in 18 months and has no deputy. Two years ago the claims system was down for 8 days, and each day without it costs about $250,000. A standby system at a second data centre would restore it within 1 day and would cost $600,000 a year. Assess whether the standby claims system is worth its cost to Harbourline. (12 marks)
practice.guidance:
Compare what the standby system costs with what it would save in an outage like the last one, then ask how often such an outage is likely. Bring in what the figures leave out, and finish with a judgement that says what it depends on.
Level 1: knowledge of business continuity or backup systems, described generally. Level 2: application — without the standby system an outage like the last one costs 8 × $250,000 = $2m; with it, recovery within 1 day costs about $250,000, a saving of $1.75m against a cost of $600,000 a year. Level 3: analysis — in a year with one outage the system more than pays for itself; in a year with none it is money spent on something unused; once branches close the claims system is the only way to claim, so the loss in customer trust is larger than the daily figure shows. Level 4: evaluation reaching a supported judgement, for example that the system is worth it because one outage every few years covers its cost and the change raises the impact of failure, provided it is tested.
A strong answer, in outline: one outage saves $1.75m against a yearly cost of $600,000; the app makes the business depend on the system entirely; so the standby system is worth it if outages happen at least every few years, and only if it is rehearsed so that it works when needed.

practice.question: Source A. Harbourline Insurance is a Hong Kong insurer with 2,400 staff, 60 branches and 7 layers of management. Many of its claims handlers have worked there for decades and take pride in spotting false claims by talking to customers face to face. After two years of falling profit, and with a new online insurer winning customers who never visit a branch, the board appointed a new chief executive. She plans to move claims onto a phone app and close 24 of the 60 branches. At present 600 handlers deal with 90,000 claims a month; after the change, 480 handlers are expected to deal with 96,000. Of the 120 handler posts that go, 70 people will retrain as app-support staff and 50 will leave. The chief executive wants the change completed in 6 months; the human resources director has proposed 24. The firm's risk register scores each risk from 1 to 5 for likelihood and for impact: typhoon closes head office (likelihood 4, impact 2); claims system fails (likelihood 3, impact 5); chief actuary leaves (likelihood 3, impact 4). The chief actuary, who prices every policy, retires in 18 months and has no deputy. Two years ago the claims system was down for 8 days, and each day without it costs about $250,000. A standby system at a second data centre would restore it within 1 day and would cost $600,000 a year. Evaluate whether the new chief executive's leadership is the most important factor in the success of the change at Harbourline. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Weigh leadership against the other key factors in change the source gives evidence for — the culture, the size of the organisation, and the time allowed — rather than writing about leadership alone. Decide what "most important" will depend on, and end with a recommendation that says what would change it.
Level 1: describes leadership or other factors in change with little reference to the source. Level 2: knowledge and application — a transformative leader sets a vision and empowers staff; the source shows a culture of long-serving handlers proud of face-to-face checks, 2,400 staff across 7 layers, and a 6-month timetable. Level 3: analysis — leadership that explains why customers are leaving and involves handlers in designing fraud checks can win support; but the culture values the old skill, a message passing down 7 layers is slow and distorted, and a short timetable leaves little time to train and explain; a change carried by one person may stall if she leaves. Level 4: evaluation — judges which factor matters most for this firm, for example that leadership matters most because it is the one factor that can shape the others (explaining, involving, setting the pace), while the culture is the biggest obstacle; the recommendation states the condition that would change it.
A strong answer, in outline: leadership can set the vision and involve staff; the culture and the size of the firm are the obstacles leadership has to overcome; speed decides whether there is time to do so; so leadership is the most important factor only if the chief executive allows enough time and involves the handlers, and a successor is identified in case she leaves.

practice.question: Source A. Harbourline Insurance is a Hong Kong insurer with 2,400 staff, 60 branches and 7 layers of management. Many of its claims handlers have worked there for decades and take pride in spotting false claims by talking to customers face to face. After two years of falling profit, and with a new online insurer winning customers who never visit a branch, the board appointed a new chief executive. She plans to move claims onto a phone app and close 24 of the 60 branches. At present 600 handlers deal with 90,000 claims a month; after the change, 480 handlers are expected to deal with 96,000. Of the 120 handler posts that go, 70 people will retrain as app-support staff and 50 will leave. The chief executive wants the change completed in 6 months; the human resources director has proposed 24. The firm's risk register scores each risk from 1 to 5 for likelihood and for impact: typhoon closes head office (likelihood 4, impact 2); claims system fails (likelihood 3, impact 5); chief actuary leaves (likelihood 3, impact 4). The chief actuary, who prices every policy, retires in 18 months and has no deputy. Two years ago the claims system was down for 8 days, and each day without it costs about $250,000. A standby system at a second data centre would restore it within 1 day and would cost $600,000 a year. Evaluate how Harbourline should manage resistance to the change from its claims handlers. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Identify the causes of resistance the source gives evidence for, because each approach suits a different cause. Then weigh the approaches against the time available and the power the handlers have, and recommend a combination rather than a single answer.
Level 1: describes ways of reducing resistance in general terms. Level 2: knowledge and application — 120 posts go (expected loss), handlers are proud of face-to-face fraud checks (loss of a valued skill, and perhaps a genuine objection), and the timetable is 6 months. Level 3: analysis — communication explains why customers are leaving; involvement lets handlers design the app's fraud checks, using what they know; retraining 70 people as app-support staff and supporting the 50 who leave addresses the loss; coercion is quick but damages trust that the next change will need. Level 4: evaluation — judges the best combination for this firm, for example that involvement matters most because the handlers' objection may be right, supported by retraining and honest communication, with coercion kept for the last few if the timetable forces it; the recommendation states what would change it.
A strong answer, in outline: the causes are job loss and a threatened skill; communication and retraining address the first, involvement the second; coercion is fast but costly in goodwill; so recommend involvement plus retraining, which needs more than a six-month timetable, and use coercion only as a last resort.

flashcards.front: What is a trigger for change?
flashcards.back: The event or pressure that starts a change. Internal triggers come from inside the firm; external triggers come from the market and the wider environment.

flashcards.front: Name four internal triggers for change.
flashcards.back: New ownership; poor business performance; a change in organisational size; a new leader.

flashcards.front: Name four external triggers for change.
flashcards.back: Customers wanting to buy in a new way; a rival's product; new technology; a change in the law or the economy.

flashcards.front: What are the effects of change to consider?
flashcards.back: Productivity, competitiveness, financial performance and the effect on each group of stakeholders.

flashcards.front: Why does profit often dip before it rises after a change?
flashcards.back: Systems, training and redundancy are paid for first, and output can fall while staff learn; the gains come later, if the change works.

flashcards.front: Incremental change or step change?
flashcards.back: Incremental change is a series of small, gradual adjustments. Step change is a large, sudden shift in what the business does or how it does it.

flashcards.front: Why does the speed of change matter?
flashcards.back: Too slow and customers or rivals move first; too fast and staff are untrained, systems untested and resistance hardens.

flashcards.front: What is organisational culture?
flashcards.back: The shared values, beliefs and habits of the people in a business: "the way things are done here".

flashcards.front: How does culture affect change?
flashcards.back: A change that fits the culture is carried along by it; one that clashes with it is resisted by people who think they are doing their jobs properly.

flashcards.front: How does the size of an organisation affect change?
flashcards.back: More layers, sites and staff slow messages and decisions, but a large firm has the money and specialists to fund the change.

flashcards.front: What is transformative leadership?
flashcards.back: Leadership that changes an organisation: setting out a vision, explaining why change is needed, inspiring staff and empowering them to deliver it.

flashcards.front: What is a limitation of transformative leadership?
flashcards.back: A change carried by one person can stall if that person leaves, and a confident leader with the wrong vision leads the firm the wrong way.

flashcards.front: What are the three sources of resistance to change?
flashcards.back: Expected loss (job, pay, status, skills); uncertainty about what the change means; genuine disagreement with the change.

flashcards.front: Name the six approaches to managing resistance.
flashcards.back: Communication and education; involvement; support and training; negotiation; co-option; coercion.

flashcards.front: What decides which approach to resistance to use?
flashcards.back: The cause of the resistance, how much time there is, and how much power the resisters have.

flashcards.front: Why is coercion a last resort?
flashcards.back: It is fast, but people who comply without agreeing lose trust and goodwill, which the next change will need.

flashcards.front: What is contingency planning?
flashcards.back: Preparing in advance for events that may not happen but would do serious harm if they did.

flashcards.front: How are key risks identified?
flashcards.back: Through risk assessment: list the risks, score each for likelihood and impact, multiply, rank, and plan for the highest first.

flashcards.front: What are the three key risks to know?
flashcards.back: Natural disasters; IT systems failure; loss of key staff.

flashcards.front: What is IT systems failure?
flashcards.back: The loss of the computer systems a business runs on, from a fault, a power cut or a cyber attack; it can stop trading and lose data.

flashcards.front: Who counts as key staff?
flashcards.back: Anyone the business depends on and cannot easily replace: a founder, a senior manager, a specialist, or the holder of key customer relationships.

flashcards.front: What is risk mitigation?
flashcards.back: Reducing the chance of harm, or the harm done if the event happens. Business continuity and succession planning are two ways.

flashcards.front: What does a business continuity plan cover?
flashcards.back: Critical activities and how fast to restore them; backups and standby systems; alternative ways of working; communication; testing.

flashcards.front: What is succession planning?
flashcards.back: Deciding in advance who could take over each critical role, and preparing them through training, mentoring and deputising.

flashcards.front: When is a contingency plan most worth its cost?
flashcards.back: When the risk is likely or its impact severe, the measure is cheap compared with the loss, or the business could not survive the loss.

mistakes.title: Treating resistance as irrational
mistakes.mistake: Writing that staff resist change because they are stubborn, and recommending that managers push harder.
mistakes.correction: Resistance usually has a cause: an expected loss, uncertainty, or a genuine objection that may be right. The response has to fit the cause.
mistakes.examTip: Name the cause of resistance for the group in the case before recommending how to manage it.

mistakes.title: Recommending one approach to resistance for every case
mistakes.mistake: Answering that "communication" is the way to overcome resistance, whatever the situation.
mistakes.correction: Communication fixes misunderstanding; it does nothing for someone who understands they will lose their job. Most changes need a combination of approaches.
mistakes.examTip: Justify each approach by the cause of resistance, the time available and the power of the people resisting.

mistakes.title: Treating speed as a strength in itself
mistakes.mistake: Praising a change for being completed quickly without asking what the speed cost.
mistakes.correction: A fast change stops the loss to rivals sooner but leaves little time to train, test and explain, so errors and resistance rise.
mistakes.examTip: Weigh the cost of being late against the cost of rushing, using the trigger in the case to judge urgency.

mistakes.title: Mixing up a risk and its mitigation
mistakes.mistake: Listing "poor business continuity planning" as one of the key risks a firm faces.
mistakes.correction: The key risks are events: natural disasters, IT systems failure, loss of key staff. Business continuity and succession planning are the responses to them.
mistakes.examTip: Keep the two apart: identify the risk first, then the plan that mitigates it.

mistakes.title: Ranking risks by likelihood alone
mistakes.mistake: Saying the most frequent risk must be the one to plan for first.
mistakes.correction: Risk assessment combines likelihood with impact. A rare event that would stop the business can outrank a frequent one that does little harm.
mistakes.examTip: Multiply or combine the two scores the case gives, then say what the scores leave out.

mistakes.title: Assuming every contingency plan is worth having
mistakes.mistake: Recommending that a firm plan for every risk it can think of.
mistakes.correction: Plans cost money and time for events that may never happen, so the effort should match the likelihood and impact of each risk.
mistakes.examTip: Compare the cost of the measure with the loss it prevents, then qualify it: how likely is the loss?

chains.title: From a trigger to the long-run result of a change
steps: A trigger arrives: new owners, falling profit, or a rival with a better product.
Managers decide on a change and announce it.
Costs rise and service may suffer while staff learn the new way of working.
If the change works, each worker produces more and the business becomes cheaper to run.
chains.result: Judge a change over time: its costs come first and its gains later.

chains.title: Identifying key risks through risk assessment
steps: List every event that could stop the business operating.
Score each event for likelihood and for impact.
Rank the events by their combined score.
Plan responses to the highest-ranked risks first.
chains.result: At Harbourline: typhoon closes head office 8, claims system fails 15, chief actuary leaves 12.

chains.title: How a succession plan is built
steps: Decide which roles the business could least afford to lose.
Pick out people inside the business who could step into each role.
Train and mentor them, and let them deputise in the role.
Hand the role over when the post-holder leaves or retires.
chains.result: A successor prepared in advance turns the loss of a key person from a crisis into a handover.

evaluation.title: Fast or gradual change?
evaluation.content: Speed is a trade. Harbourline's chief executive wants the change done in 6 months; the human resources director proposes 24. Faster change stops customers leaving for the online rival sooner. Slower change gives time to train 70 people, test the app and involve handlers in designing it, which reduces errors and resistance. The deciding question is how fast the trigger is moving compared with how fast the business can safely change. Starting in a few branches can buy some of both.

evaluation.title: Which key factor matters most?
evaluation.content: Culture, size, speed, resistance and leadership all shape whether a change succeeds, and they interact. A strong culture that values the old way makes resistance deeper; a large organisation makes communication slower; a short timetable leaves less room for either to be addressed. Leadership is often the factor that can act on the others, by explaining, involving and setting a realistic pace, which is why a strong answer judges it against the others rather than in isolation.

evaluation.title: Is contingency planning worth what it costs?
evaluation.content: A plan is paid for now, against a loss that may never come. Harbourline's standby claims system costs $600,000 a year and would cut an outage like the last one from $2m to $250,000. That is worth it if such outages happen every few years and the business could not do without the system; it is less clear for a rare, minor risk. A plan that has never been rehearsed may fail when it is needed, so part of its cost is testing it.
